stories.headline: Update: Iran Vows to 'Punish' U.S. After Heavy Wave of American Strikes; Civilian Deaths Reported
stories.summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard vowed Thursday to "punish the aggressor" after the U.S. military completed a "heavy wave of strikes" against targets across Iran overnight, the latest escalation in a cycle of retaliatory attacks. The strikes, which included what U.S. officials described as "a very broad target set," were launched in response to an Iranian ballistic missile attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. Iranian media reported that a couple and their two-year-old child were killed in strikes on Qeshm island.

The new U.S. strikes represent the first since President Trump paused operations last Friday to allow negotiations another chance. Iran has also struck three ships in the Strait of Hormuz and rejected Oman's proposal for managing the waterway. The Revolutionary Guard extended its threats to Gulf nations assisting the United States, raising fears of a broader regional conflagration.

Diplomatically, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman conveyed a message to Vice President Vance that Riyadh favors de-escalation despite participating in joint U.S.-Saudi strikes on pro-Iranian militias in Iraq. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu expressed skepticism about any deal with Iran during his Tuesday meeting with Trump, and discussed increasing economic pressure through "kinetic and non-kinetic means."

The conflict continues to generate domestic political pressure, with congressional Democrats demanding answers over reports that wounded U.S. soldiers went more than a week without adequate hospital care following a March drone strike in Kuwait. Trump has been described by sources as "exasperated" as top officials remain divided on strategy.

stories.headline: Democratic Socialist Candidates Surge in Michigan and Wisconsin Primaries, Signaling Establishment Collapse
stories.summary:
With Michigan's Senate primary on August 4 and Wisconsin's gubernatorial primary on August 11, Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidates are poised to capture both nominations, according to multiple polls. Abdul El-Sayed leads Michigan's race by a wide margin over establishment candidate Haley Stevens, while Wisconsin's Francesca Hong holds 38 percent support, more than double her nearest competitor, former Lt. Governor Mandela Barnes.

The DSA surge extends beyond these two contests. Earlier this year, DSA-affiliated or socialist candidates defeated multiple long-serving incumbents, including Representative Diana DeGette of Colorado (a 15-term incumbent), Representative Adriano Espaillat of New York, and incumbent Dan Goldman in New York's 10th district. Three-term Colorado Senator Michael Bennet also lost his gubernatorial primary to the state attorney general.

Analysts are debating whether the results represent a genuine leftward ideological shift or, as some commentators have reframed it, a collapse of Democratic establishment credibility. A Vox analysis by Astead Herndon argues the phenomenon may be less about the rise of socialism than about rank-and-file Democratic voters losing faith in party leadership after years of perceived failures.

Conservatives view the trend as evidence of an increasingly radical Democratic Party moving out of step with the American mainstream, while progressives argue it reflects a long-overdue accountability reckoning for an establishment that failed its base on healthcare, economic inequality, and other core issues. The outcomes of the August primaries will serve as major indicators of which faction controls the party's future direction.

stories.headline: UEFA and CONCACAF Threaten World Cup Boycott Over FIFA Plan to Sell Stakes to Private Investors
stories.summary:
European football's 55 member associations voted Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups, if FIFA proceeds with a plan to sell minority stakes in its tournaments to private investors. The vote came at an emergency meeting convened to address the proposal announced earlier this week by FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who seeks to create a commercial subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise, in which external investors could acquire non-controlling stakes.

CONCACAF, the governing body for North and Central American football whose 41 member associations include the host nations of this year's World Cup, also formally rejected the Infantino proposal on Thursday. Combined, UEFA and CONCACAF members represent 96 of the 211 FIFA associations, meaning Infantino needs to secure an additional 10 votes beyond the remaining federations to reach the 106-vote threshold required for approval.

Infantino has written to FIFA members offering $40 million to associations that back his plan and set a September 19 deadline for accessing an initial $20 million tranche, a tactic that critics including Scottish football executive James McAllister characterized as "blackmail." In a video released Wednesday, Infantino defended the proposal as "an offer, not an obligation."

The first practical test of the boycott threat would come in October, when Women's World Cup play-offs are scheduled. The standoff represents one of the gravest governance crises in world football history, pitting the sport's most powerful regional confederations directly against the global body's leadership.

stories.headline: Hungary's Only Nuclear Plant to Shut Down as Danube Hits 30-Year Low, Romania Also Affected
stories.summary:
Hungary's sole nuclear power plant at Paks will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time in its history because the River Danube has fallen to its lowest levels in 30 years, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced Thursday. The Soviet-era facility relies on Danube water for cooling, but water levels have dropped so drastically that the plant's suction nozzles can no longer reach the river. Magyar warned that Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday, compounded by a week-long heat wave with temperatures around 37 degrees Celsius driving peak electricity demand.

Romania is facing a parallel crisis: one of its two nuclear reactors at the Cernavoda plant, which provides roughly 20 percent of the country's electricity, has already been shut down due to low Danube levels, and operators were struggling Thursday to keep the second reactor running. If both reactors go offline, Romania will also be temporarily without any nuclear power generation. The Danube's average flow into Romania in July is approximately 4,700 cubic meters per second; this week it measured just 1,600 and was forecast to fall further.

The crisis reflects a summer of extreme drought and heat across Europe. Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the season, and the Danube has reached record or near-record lows across multiple countries including Serbia and Romania. Magyar asked citizens to reduce energy consumption between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., particularly air conditioning and electric vehicle charging, and warned that rotating blackouts remained possible if voluntary measures proved insufficient.

The European continent has been warming at roughly twice the global average rate, according to the Copernicus climate service, intensifying pressure on water supplies, power systems, and infrastructure simultaneously. The Paks plant provides a significant share of Hungary's electricity, making its shutdown a major test of the country's grid resilience and energy import capacity in the middle of a heat emergency.

stories.headline: Father of Apalachee High School Shooter Sentenced to 15 Years in Landmark Parental Liability Case
stories.summary:
A Georgia judge sentenced Colin Gray, 55, to 15 years in prison Thursday for his role in the 2024 Apalachee High School shooting that killed four people — two students and two teachers — carried out by his then-16-year-old son Colt Gray. Judge Nicholas Primm handed down concurrent 15-year sentences for each second-degree murder conviction and 10-year sentences for each involuntary manslaughter conviction, rejecting prosecutors' request for the maximum 80-year term. The rifle used in the attack was a Christmas gift from Colin Gray to his son.

The case marks only the third time in U.S. history that a parent has been held criminally responsible for a mass shooting committed by their child, according to CBS News. Prosecutors argued that Colin Gray ignored escalating warning signs, including a notebook detailing his son's plans to shoot classmates and the fact that the boy had been questioned by police about online shooting threats just seven months before receiving the rifle. "After seeing sign after sign of his son's deteriorating mental state, the defendant had sufficient warning that his son was a bomb just waiting to go off," a prosecutor told jurors during the trial.

Judge Primm told Gray directly before sentencing that he had "failed as a parent," citing his failure to send his son to counseling, monitor his online activity, or secure firearms in the home. At the same time, Primm acknowledged that Gray "didn't seek to harm anyone" and "didn't pull a trigger," factors that weighed against the maximum sentence sought by the state. The defense had sought a 10-year sentence and attempted to shift moral responsibility to the shooter himself.

Colt Gray pleaded guilty to the murders last week and will be sentenced separately. The Apalachee case has become a reference point in a national legal debate over parental accountability for juvenile mass shootings, a framework that gained traction following the conviction of the parents of the 2021 Oxford, Michigan school shooter.

stories.headline: Update: Senate Panel Delays Vote on Blanche Attorney General Nomination as Trump Threatens to Pull Pick
stories.summary:
The Senate Judiciary Committee postponed a scheduled Thursday vote on Todd Blanche's nomination as attorney general after two Republican senators — John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — continued to withhold support over the Trump administration's controversial $10 billion IRS tax settlement. The settlement, which included audit immunity for Trump and his family, and a now-scrapped $1.776 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund," has drawn bipartisan criticism. Cornyn accused the Justice Department of "stonewalling" and said the ball was "in Blanche's court."

President Trump escalated the standoff Thursday, saying he may temporarily withdraw Blanche's nomination and resubmit it after Cornyn and Tillis — both of whom are leaving office in January — are gone. "Todd Blanche is a STAR," Trump posted on social media, framing the two senators' objections as obstruction. The Justice Department sent new written language to Cornyn and Tillis Wednesday evening in an attempt to satisfy their demands, though no resolution had been reached as of Thursday.

Cornyn and Tillis have specifically demanded written assurances that the Anti-Weaponization Fund is permanently dead and that the audit immunity deal covers only existing audits, not future tax filings. The core dispute reflects broader Republican unease about the administration's use of the Justice Department to settle the president's personal legal matters.

Supporters of Blanche argue he is qualified for the role and that the senators' objections are being used as leverage in an internal GOP power struggle. Critics, including Democrats, contend the underlying IRS settlement represents an improper use of government power and that the confirmation fight has exposed a rare fracture within the Republican caucus less than 100 days before midterm elections.

stories.headline: U.S. Economy Grows Sluggish 1.5% in Second Quarter as Inflation Remains Above Fed Target
stories.summary:
The U.S. economy expanded at an annualized rate of 1.5% from April through June, the Commerce Department reported Thursday, a deceleration from 2.1% growth in the first quarter and below economists' expectations. Rising imports — up 11.5%, partly driven by a surge in AI-related chip purchases — subtracted 1.5 percentage points from GDP. Consumer spending, which accounts for roughly 70% of economic activity, rose at a robust 3.2% annual pace, up sharply from 0.5% in the first quarter.

Inflation remained stubbornly elevated. The Federal Reserve's preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 3.7% year-over-year in June, down from 4.1% in May but still well above the Fed's 2% target. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, stood at 3.3% annually. The Fed on Wednesday voted to hold interest rates steady for the fifth consecutive meeting, though three officials dissented in favor of a rate increase.

Business investment excluding housing rose at an 8.4% pace, reflecting continued heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. "The consumer rescued the quarter," said Olu Sonola of Fitch Ratings, adding that the AI investment boom's import-heavy nature limits its direct boost to GDP figures.

The data lands with particular political weight, coming fewer than 100 days before November's midterm elections. Americans have reported persistent economic pessimism driven by elevated prices and energy costs tied to the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict, which has pushed gasoline prices higher. The sluggish headline growth figure, combined with sticky inflation, complicates the political environment for Republicans defending congressional majorities.

stories.headline: Fauci Invokes Fifth Amendment Over 100 Times at Republican-Led Senate COVID Origins Hearing
stories.summary:
Former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination more than 100 times Wednesday before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky. The hearing focused on the origins of COVID-19, allegations that U.S.-funded research in China contributed to the pandemic, and Fauci's handling of the public health response — allegations Fauci has denied.

Fauci's lawyers advised him to decline all questions under oath, arguing that his answers could expose him to new legal risks. Although former President Joe Biden granted Fauci a preemptive pardon in January 2025, Republicans contend it does not shield him from perjury charges for false statements made after that date. In a brief opening statement, Fauci accused Paul of having an "obsession" with prosecuting him and argued the hearing was not legitimate congressional oversight but rather an attempt to build a criminal case.

Republican senators including Paul and Ted Cruz called for contempt charges and possible perjury prosecution following the hearing. Paul announced plans for a formal contempt vote. Fauci's supporters argued he was exercising a constitutionally protected right in the face of what they characterized as a politically motivated pursuit, and noted that the pardon's scope makes actual prosecution difficult.

The hearing marks a significant escalation in a years-long political battle over pandemic accountability. The 85-year-old Fauci, who served as the public face of the U.S. COVID-19 response and advised seven presidents over nearly four decades, has become a central figure in conservative efforts to relitigate pandemic-era policies including mask mandates, vaccine recommendations, and school closures.

stories.headline: Pennsylvania Medicaid Begins Covering Elective Abortions for First Time Since 1985
stories.summary:
Pennsylvania's Medicaid program has begun covering elective abortions following an April ruling by the state's Commonwealth Court, which found that existing restrictions on taxpayer funding of abortion violate the state's Equal Rights Amendment. The change makes Pennsylvania the seventh state in the past decade to expand Medicaid abortion coverage, joining Illinois, Maine, Colorado, Delaware, Nevada, and Rhode Island.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, a Republican, is appealing the Commonwealth Court ruling to the State Supreme Court. However, five of the seven justices on that court are elected Democrats, making a reversal of the lower court decision unlikely, according to analysts.

Supporters of the ruling argue that denying Medicaid coverage for abortion services discriminates against low-income women and violates equal protection principles enshrined in the state constitution. Opponents, including anti-abortion advocates and the attorney general, argue that taxpayer funding of abortion is a policy that should be decided through the legislature, not the courts, and that academic research links public funding to higher abortion rates.

The case is being closely watched nationally as a test of how state equal rights amendments can be used to expand abortion access independent of federal law, particularly since the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 Dobbs decision returned abortion regulation to individual states.

stories.headline: Update: Europe Wildfires — Evacuees Return to Parts of Spain as France Battles Ongoing Blazes With International Help
stories.summary:
Residents of ten towns in Spain were permitted to return home on Wednesday after evacuation orders were lifted following progress in controlling blazes near Madrid, which officials described as among the worst the region has ever seen. In France, tens of thousands remain displaced across the southwest, with nearly 80,000 people still unable to return to their homes in the Gironde region as fires continued to burn after more than a week.

French firefighting efforts have drawn hundreds of volunteers alongside professional crews, with aerial tankers and helicopters deploying water and fire retardant across the Bordeaux area. Belgium has sent backup personnel to assist. Two firefighters died battling a separate wildfire on the Greek island of Crete, adding to the human toll of the broader European fire emergency.

Economic damage is mounting significantly. The head of the Bordeaux regional chamber of commerce described a dual "physical and economic apocalypse," with businesses destroyed at the height of summer tourist season. In the village of Le Porge, 183 homes were lost, with one official comparing the destruction to a bombed-out Ukrainian village.

This update reflects new developments including the lifting of evacuation orders in Spain, the deaths of two firefighters in Greece, and continued escalation in France — all occurring Wednesday. Temperatures are forecast to rise further, increasing the risk of new ignitions.

stories.headline: Elon Musk's xAI Sues Minnesota Over First-in-Nation AI Nudification Ban
stories.summary:
Elon Musk's artificial intelligence company xAI filed a federal lawsuit Monday challenging Minnesota's law banning "nudification" technology — AI tools that generate fake nude images of real people. The law, signed in May, is set to take effect Saturday and would make Minnesota the first state to outlaw the underlying technology itself, rather than merely penalizing those who use it to create non-consensual images.

In its 38-page complaint, xAI said it does not dispute the state's interest in preventing non-consensual AI-generated nude imagery, but argues the law is overbroad and unconstitutional. The company contends the law lacks a "safe harbor" for platforms that make good-faith compliance efforts, covers images created with the depicted person's consent, and imposes penalties of up to $500,000 per violation. xAI's Grok chatbot and image generator are available through the social media platform X.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said his office had not yet been served with the lawsuit but defended the law in strong terms, stating that "AI nudification robs the target of their dignity and can cause immense harm on an emotional, personal, and professional level." He said the debate over this particular technology was not among the "worthy debates" on AI policy.

The lawsuit sets up a significant First Amendment test case for state regulation of AI tools. A similar California law targeting election deepfakes was blocked by courts on free speech grounds. Minnesota's nudification law survived an earlier 2025 court challenge brought by Musk's company, and the outcome of this latest challenge could influence how other states approach AI content regulation.

stories.headline: Nicaragua's Ortega Proposes Extending Presidential Term as Authoritarian Grip Tightens
stories.summary:
Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega, who has ruled continuously since 2007, has proposed extending the presidential term by one additional year through a new round of constitutional reforms. The government-controlled National Assembly is expected to approve the measure in September. The same package of reforms would bar opposition figures deemed "traitors" or "coup plotters" by the government from running for office.

Ortega's government has a lengthy record of altering constitutional rules in its favor. In 2014 the National Assembly eliminated presidential term limits entirely; in 2024 it extended the presidential term from five to six years. Earlier this year, the legislature also approved naming Ortega's wife, Rosario Murillo, as "co-president," positioning her to assume the presidency if the 80-year-old, believed to be in declining health, is declared "permanently absent."

The United Nations human rights chief has warned that repression has deepened under Ortega's rule, with the rule of law steadily eroded and political dissidents persecuted, jailed, exiled, and stripped of citizenship. The 2021 presidential election was widely regarded as non-competitive after credible opposition candidates were detained, disqualified, or forced into exile ahead of the vote.

The proposed extension further entrenches what international observers describe as one of the Western Hemisphere's most authoritarian governments. With no meaningful opposition permitted inside Nicaragua and dissidents targeted even abroad, there is little domestic mechanism to challenge the reforms.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Resume Strikes as Brief Pause Collapses; Russian Missile Lands in Poland
stories.summary:
The fragile pause in the U.S.-Iran conflict has shattered after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. military base in Jordan in what CENTCOM described as an "attempted surprise attack." All missiles were intercepted with no U.S. casualties, but the attack prompted a fresh American retaliatory barrage lasting roughly two hours that struck "dozens" of Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps targets, including sites on Qeshm Island and near Bushehr. The U.S. and Saudi Arabia also conducted joint strikes on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and Jordan reported intercepting additional missiles targeting its territory.

The renewed fighting has raised fears of a return to all-out war after weeks of escalation since the conflict began February 28. Oil prices climbed back above $91 per barrel on the renewed hostilities, and stocks fell sharply with the Dow dropping more than 1,150 points. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, meeting with President Trump at the White House, expressed skepticism about the prospects for a deal and discussed increasing economic pressure on Iran through "kinetic and non-kinetic means." Saudi Arabia, despite participating in the Iraq strikes, sent its defense minister to Washington to reiterate that Riyadh still favors de-escalation.

In a separate but related development, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile likely crossed into Polish territory overnight, leaving a 10-meter-wide crater in a field in eastern Poland near the Ukrainian border during a massive Russian assault on Lviv that killed at least eight people. Poland scrambled fighter jets and is conducting pyrotechnical analysis to confirm the missile's origin. No casualties were reported on Polish soil, but the incident triggered emergency consultations with European leaders and raised acute concerns about NATO airspace integrity.

A Russian missile landing on NATO territory — even without casualties — carries significant alliance implications and echoes a similar incident in November 2022. Ukraine's acting foreign minister confirmed the missile crossed into Poland as part of Russia's wider strike campaign. Polish officials said they were prepared to shoot it down had it continued its flight path.

stories.headline: Update: Federal Reserve Holds Rates for Fifth Straight Meeting in Divided Vote as Iran Conflict Fuels Inflation Pressure
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged Wednesday in a 9-3 vote, marking the fifth consecutive meeting without a rate change. Three dissenting members — Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, and a third official — voted in favor of a quarter-point rate increase, the first three-way dissent in over a decade. Fed officials indicated they expect inflation to ease, but the decision came under intense scrutiny given persistent inflation pressure exacerbated by rising energy prices tied to the U.S.-Iran conflict.

The hold disappointed markets: the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 1,150 points, its worst single-day drop since the April 2025 "Liberation Day" tariff announcement, while the S&P 500 declined 1.52 percent. U.S. 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since 2007 following the decision. Brent crude oil traded near $91 per barrel, well off its recent highs above $101 but rising again as fighting between the U.S. and Iran resumed.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has made taming inflation a stated priority, but his reluctance to embrace higher borrowing costs has drawn criticism from within the central bank and on Wall Street. The three dissenting votes signal growing internal pressure to act more aggressively. Some analysts noted that China's withdrawal from global oil markets as a buyer has helped contain the worst potential price spikes from the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.headline: Update: Rushdie Attacker Convicted of Terrorism Charges, Now Faces Possible Life Sentence
stories.summary:
Hadi Matar, already serving a 25-year state prison sentence for the 2022 stabbing of author Salman Rushdie, was convicted Wednesday in a New York federal court on additional charges of engaging in transnational terrorism and providing material support to Hezbollah. Prosecutors argued Matar was motivated by a 2006 speech by then-Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah calling for enforcement of the 1989 fatwa issued by Iran's supreme leader calling for Rushdie's death, and that he had plotted the attack for two years.

Rushdie himself testified at the Buffalo, New York trial, describing being stabbed 15 times on stage and lifting the darkened lens of his glasses to reveal his injured eye, which left him partially blind. "I was on the stage, lying down, with an enormous pool of blood all around me," Rushdie testified, adding the knife came "within millimetres from my brain." A firefighter's immediate medical response, Rushdie said, saved his life.

Defense attorneys argued the attack was not terrorism-motivated and questioned Rushdie about anticipated backlash to his 1988 novel "The Satanic Verses." Rushdie rejected the framing: "I don't believe the book is on trial. Somebody else is on trial." Matar now faces a potential life sentence when sentenced on the federal conviction, on top of his existing state term.

stories.headline: Ugandan Opposition Leader Kizza Besigye Collapses in Court, Hospitalized Unconscious in ICU
stories.summary:
Veteran Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye, 70, collapsed and lost consciousness in a Kampala courtroom Wednesday while objecting to state-appointed lawyers being assigned to represent him in his treason trial. His wife, Winnie Byanyima — who heads UNAIDS — said he was admitted to the ICU at Mulago National Referral Hospital, describing him as "unconscious, unable to speak, and unresponsive even to a pain stimulus."

Besigye has been held in detention since November 2024 after being abducted from Kenya and returned to Uganda, where he and an aide face treason charges they deny, alleging they plotted to overthrow President Yoweri Museveni. Treason is a capital offense in Uganda. His primary lawyer was jailed last month on related charges, and a Kenyan attorney brought in to represent him was barred from entering the country.

Family members and human rights groups have called for Besigye's release on medical grounds, with his son writing an open letter to President Museveni and the army chief appealing for humanitarian consideration. Besigye refused treatment from government medical personnel but his sister, who is also a doctor, was eventually allowed access to him. The ICU ward is guarded by heavily armed security officers.
